name: Qara Qoyunlu
info: A Turkoman dynasty ruling from Tabriz over Azerbaijan, Armenia, western Iran and Iraq between the Timurids and the Aq Qoyunlu, remembered for the Blue Mosque of Tabriz and its tilework.

facts.capital: Mosul (as Jalayirid vassals), then Tabriz from 1406–1410
facts.founder: Qara Yusuf, who won independence from the Jalayirids in 1410; the tribe's earlier leaders were Birdi Khwaja, Bayram Khwaja and Qara Mahammad
facts.predecessor: The Jalayirid Sultanate (overlords from about 1375), the Artuqids of Mardin and the Timurid governors of Azerbaijan
facts.successor: The Aq Qoyunlu under Uzun Hasan, who conquered Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran by 1468

t: Qara Yusuf returned from Mamluk captivity to defeat the Timurids at Nakhchivan in 1406 and Sardrud in 1408, and by taking Tabriz and Baghdad in 1410 freed the Qara Qoyunlu from the Jalayirids.
Jahan Shah (1436–1467) became independent on Shah Rukh's death in 1447, conquered Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd in 1452–1453 and occupied Herat for some months in 1458.
The Qara Qoyunlu court wrote to the Timurids and Ottomans in Persian and to the Mamluks in Arabic, and Jahan Shah styled himself Padishah-i Iran, King of Kings of Iran.
dyk: Sultan Quli, founder of the Qutb Shahi Sultanate of Golconda in southern India in 1518, was a fourth-generation descendant of the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Qara Iskander.
ev: Qara Mahammad invades Mardin and takes the submission of its Artuqid ruler Majd al-Din Isa, who becomes a vassal.
Timur defeats the Qara Qoyunlu; Qara Yusuf flees to the Mamluk Sultanate, where an-Nasir Faraj imprisons him together with the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad.
Qara Yusuf crushes the Timurids Abu Bakr and Miran Shah at the Battle of Sardrud on 20 April; Miran Shah is killed.
Qara Yusuf conquers Tabriz, executes Shaykh Uways Jalayir, captures Baghdad and takes control of Armenia; the Qara Qoyunlu are independent.
Qara Yusuf dies in December; his sons fight for the succession and Shah Rukh invades, occupying Tabriz briefly in 1421.
On Shah Rukh's death Jahan Shah throws off Timurid vassalage, takes the titles sultan and khan and seizes Sultaniya, Hamadan and Qazvin.
Jahan Shah advances to Herat and holds the Timurid capital for some months, until Hasan Ali's revolt and Abu Said's march on Tabriz force him back.
Jahan Shah is killed at the Battle of Chapakchur after his failed attack on Aq Qoyunlu Diyarbakır; by 1468 Uzun Hasan has conquered Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran.

sections.foundation:
The Qara Qoyunlu, the Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman, Muslim and culturally Persianate dynasty whose name most likely came from the black sheep painted on their flags, or from the colour of their flocks. The ruling family descended from the Baharlu of the Yıwa tribe of the Oghuz Turks, who by the fourteenth century held lands north of Lake Van and around Mosul in Upper Mesopotamia. Around them gathered the Saadlu, Karamanlu, Alpaut, Agacheri, Dukharlu, Jagirlu and Hajilu tribes, from Nakhchivan and Ganja to Maraş, Erzurum and Ardabil; their own traditions say they came to Anatolia from Central Asia with the Mongol conquest.

In the fourteenth century they lived in the shadow of the Jalayirid Sultanate of Baghdad and Tabriz. In 1366 Shaykh Uways Jalayir defeated their leader Birdi Khwaja at Mosul and his brother Bayram Khwaja at the battle of Mush, and from about 1375 the Qara Qoyunlu were Jalayirid vassals ruling from Mosul. Qara Mahammad invaded Mardin in 1384 and took the submission of its Artuqid ruler. Then came Timur: in 1400 the Timurids defeated the Qara Qoyunlu and Qara Yusuf fled to the Mamluk Sultanate, where Sultan an-Nasir Faraj, unwilling to anger Timur, imprisoned him with the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad Jalayir. In prison the two agreed that Ahmad should keep Baghdad and Qara Yusuf have Azerbaijan, Ahmad adopted Qara Yusuf's son Pirbudag, and both were released on Timur's death in 1405.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Qara Qoyunlu were a loose confederation of pastoral tribes whose wealth lay in flocks; mutton was the staple of their diet. Their rule over settled peoples rested on the taxes and labour of Armenians, Persians, Kurds and Arabs in the towns and plains they held from Mosul to Tabriz, Baghdad, Isfahan and Shiraz. The Armenian historian Tovma Metsopetsi records heavy taxes on the Armenians after the conquest of 1410 but relatively peaceful early years in which some towns were rebuilt. Under Qara Iskander, however, Armenia was made a “desert” and subjected to “devastation and plunder, to slaughter, and captivity”; many Armenians were taken captive and sold into slavery in his wars with the Timurids, Jahan Shah's forces sacked the Tatev monastery in Syunik, and many left the land.

Jahan Shah also allotted land to Armenian lords, rebuilt churches and in 1441 approved the move of the Catholicos of the Armenian Apostolic Church to Etchmiadzin Cathedral. Georgia suffered repeated raids from Qara Yusuf's attack on Akhaltsikhe in 1416 onward. The cities kept their crafts: Tabriz was a centre of artists and calligraphers, a group of whom Baysunghur carried off to Herat in 1421. The court was Persianate, and Qara Qoyunlu rule speeded the process by which Azerbaijan and parts of Fars became ethnically and linguistically Turkic. Shia Islam spread in their lands through Shaykh Junayd of the Safavid order and the Musha'sha' in Khuzistan.
sections.military:
The Qara Qoyunlu fought as Turkoman tribal cavalry. Having lost to the Jalayirids in 1366 and to Timur in 1400, Qara Yusuf returned from Egypt in 1405, forced Timur's governor of Van to submit and captured the viceroy Altamış. He defeated the Timurid prince Abu Bakr at the Battle of Nakhchivan on 14 October 1406 and reoccupied Tabriz; when Abu Bakr and his father Miran Shah tried to recover Azerbaijan, he crushed them at the Battle of Sardrud on 20 April 1408, where Miran Shah was killed. In 1409 he took Mardin, the Artuqids' last stronghold; in 1410 he conquered Tabriz, had Shaykh Uways Jalayir executed and captured Baghdad, and Armenia fell under his control.

Timurid power did not accept the loss. After Qara Yusuf's death in 1420 Shah Rukh beat Qara Iskander in 1420–21 and briefly occupied Tabriz, beat him again in 1429, and in a third expedition of 1434–35 installed Iskander's brother Jahan Shah as vassal. Jahan Shah, independent after Shah Rukh's death in 1447, seized Saveh, Qum, Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd in 1452–1453, and in the summer of 1458 held Herat for some months until his son Hasan Ali's revolt and Abu Said's march on Tabriz forced him back. Princes and beys kept their own trained and salaried soldiers, the nökers. The last war was with the Aq Qoyunlu: Jahan Shah's attempt to take Diyarbakır from them in 1466 ended in catastrophe, and he died at the Battle of Chapakchur in 1467.
sections.governance:
The Qara Qoyunlu state was organised on the model of its predecessors, the Jalayirids and the Ilkhanids. Jahan Shah, crowned on 19 April 1438 with the epithet Muzaffar al-Din, took the titles sultan and khan on becoming independent in 1447 and styled himself Padishah-i Iran and King of Kings of Iran. The court used Persian for diplomacy, poetry and administration: letters to the Timurids and Ottomans were written in Persian and those to the Mamluks in Arabic. Provinces were governed by şehzades, princes of the house, and by beys, each with a smaller divan, the beys' posts generally passing from father to son; in the cities officials called darugha handled finance and administration and held political power.

The dynasty's weakness was its own family. Qara Yusuf's death in 1420 set his descendants fighting, and the Timurids exploited the quarrel to replace Iskander with Jahan Shah. Jahan Shah's sons rebelled in turn: Hasan Ali, imprisoned at Maku, rose in 1458; Pir Budaq, governor of Shiraz, sought independence, was spared at his mother's request and moved to Baghdad, rebelled again and was defeated in 1464 and executed on his father's orders. On religion the evidence is mixed: Vladimir Minorsky saw the Qara Qoyunlu adopting Shia Islam as a unifying ideology for a loose tribal confederation, forerunners of the Safavids, yet their coins named the four caliphs, and Bosworth finds “no strong evidence” of Shia sympathies.
sections.impact:
The Qara Qoyunlu's lasting work is in brick and tile. Jahan Shah commissioned the northern iwan of the Darb-e Imam in Isfahan in 1453, two years after taking the city, “a masterpiece of tile decoration”; he restored the eastern iwan of the Jameh Mosque of Yazd in 1457, and a foundation of his wife built the Blue Mosque in Tabriz, finished in 1465, whose “unrivalled” underglaze tiles and mosaics in cobalt blue with incised gold and white covered walls, exterior and dome. This Turkmen tilework travelled: the blue-and-white tiles of Mamluk Syria and Egypt and of Ottoman Bursa and Edirne are thought to be the work of itinerant artists from Tabriz, and “Abdallah of Tabriz” signed the tiles of the Dome of the Rock for Sultan Süleyman in 1545–1552.

In the arts of the book Pir Budaq, governor of Fars and Baghdad, sponsored innovations in nasta'liq calligraphy and finely illustrated manuscripts. Jahan Shah wrote poetry in Azerbaijani and Persian, and Abu Bakr Tehrani's Kitab-i Diyarbakriyya chronicled the dynasty in Persian. Politically the dynasty broke the Jalayirids, kept western Iran out of Timurid hands and, by Minorsky's account, prepared the Shia ground the Safavids built on; its people's language became Azerbaijani. Its descendants ruled far away: Sultan Quli, a fourth-generation descendant of Qara Iskander, founded the Qutb Shahi Sultanate of Golconda in 1518, and Bairam Khan of the Baharlu commanded the Mughal army.
sections.decline:
Jahan Shah won much territory, but his reign was troubled by rebellious sons and by the near-autonomous rulers of Baghdad, whom he expelled in 1464. The eastern campaigns had shown the limits of Turkoman power: Herat could be held only for months in 1458, and peace with the Timurids was sealed by marrying a daughter to Sultan Muhammad bin Baysonqor. The deadlier rival stood in the west. The Aq Qoyunlu, the White Sheep Turkomans of Diyarbakır, were the Qara Qoyunlu's old enemies and, probably out of that enmity, rejected the heterodox religious currents their rivals tolerated. In 1466 Jahan Shah attempted to take Diyarbakır from them; the campaign ended in catastrophic failure, and in 1467 he was killed at the Battle of Chapakchur.

His death brought the collapse of Qara Qoyunlu control across the Middle East. Hasan Ali, the son who had twice rebelled against him, came to power but was killed by Uzun Hasan, and by 1468 the Aq Qoyunlu under Uzun Hasan (1452–1478), at the height of their power, had defeated the Qara Qoyunlu and conquered Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran. What survived were monuments and people: the mausoleum of the Blue Mosque in Tabriz went on being built under the Aq Qoyunlu into the 1480s, the Tabriz school of tilework worked for Mamluks and Ottomans into the mid-sixteenth century, the Armenian Catholicosate stayed at Etchmiadzin, and the Baharlu carried the name east to Golconda and the Mughal court.

summary: The Qara Qoyunlu, a Turkoman confederation from the lands around Lake Van and Mosul, threw off Jalayirid overlordship under Qara Yusuf in 1410, held Tabriz, Baghdad and Armenia against the Timurids, and under Jahan Shah ruled from Azerbaijan to Fars and briefly Herat, before Jahan Shah's death at Chapakchur in 1467 handed their lands to the Aq Qoyunlu.
references: H. R. Roemer, “The Turkmen dynasties”, in The Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 6: The Timurid and Safavid Periods (Cambridge University Press, 1986)
V. Minorsky, “Jihān-Shāh Qara-Qoyunlu and His Poetry (Turkmenica, 9)”, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 16 (1954)
Clifford E. Bosworth, The New Islamic Dynasties (Columbia University Press, 1996)

Dickran Kouymjian, “Armenia from the fall of the Cilician Kingdom (1375) to the forced emigration under Shah Abbas”, in The Armenian People From Ancient to Modern Times, vol. II (Palgrave Macmillan, 2004)
R. M. Savory, “The Struggle for Supremacy in Persia after the death of Tīmūr”, Der Islam 40 (De Gruyter)
R. Quiring-Zoche, “Āq Qoyunlū”, Encyclopædia Iranica, vol. II, fasc. 2 (1986)

pointDescs.1374: The Qara Qoyunlu, beaten by Shaykh Uways Jalayir at Mosul and Mush in 1366, become vassals of the Jalayirid Sultanate from about 1375, their leading tribe ruling from Mosul.
pointDescs.1384: Qara Mahammad invades Mardin and makes its Artuqid ruler Majd al-Din Isa a vassal.
pointDescs.1400: Timur defeats the Qara Qoyunlu; Qara Yusuf flees to Egypt and is imprisoned by an-Nasir Faraj with Ahmad Jalayir, until both are freed on Timur's death in 1405.
pointDescs.1406: Qara Yusuf defeats the Timurid Abu Bakr at the Battle of Nakhchivan on 14 October and reoccupies Tabriz.
pointDescs.1408: At the Battle of Sardrud on 20 April Qara Yusuf crushes Abu Bakr and Miran Shah, who is killed; Azerbaijan is secured.
pointDescs.1410: Qara Yusuf conquers Tabriz, executes Shaykh Uways Jalayir and captures Baghdad; Armenia comes under Qara Qoyunlu control and the dynasty is independent of the Jalayirids.
pointDescs.1420: Qara Yusuf dies in December; his sons fight over the succession and Shah Rukh defeats Qara Iskander in 1420–21.
pointDescs.1421: The Timurids briefly occupy Tabriz, and Baysunghur carries its artists and calligraphers off to Herat; Iskander's wars with the Timurids devastate Armenia.
pointDescs.1435: Shah Rukh's third expedition (1434–35) prevails; he installs Iskander's brother Jahan Shah as his vassal, and Jahan Shah is crowned on 19 April 1438.
pointDescs.1447: Shah Rukh dies; Jahan Shah becomes an independent sultan and khan and takes Sultaniya, Hamadan and Qazvin from the Timurids.
pointDescs.1453: Jahan Shah seizes Saveh, Qum, Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd in 1452–1453 and dedicates the northern iwan of the Darb-e Imam in Isfahan; Pir Budaq governs Shiraz.
pointDescs.1458: Jahan Shah occupies Herat for some months, the dynasty's furthest reach, before Hasan Ali's revolt and Abu Said's march on Tabriz force him home.
pointDescs.1464: Pir Budaq's second rebellion in Baghdad is crushed and he is executed; Jahan Shah expels the near-autonomous rulers of Baghdad. The Blue Mosque of Tabriz is finished in 1465.
pointDescs.1467: Jahan Shah's attack on Aq Qoyunlu Diyarbakır in 1466 fails catastrophically and he is killed at the Battle of Chapakchur; Qara Qoyunlu control collapses.
pointDescs.1468: Hasan Ali is killed by Uzun Hasan, and the Aq Qoyunlu conquer Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran.

notes: The register's start 1374 matches the article's 'from about 1374 to 1468'; the article dates the Jalayirid vassalage 'from about 1375', and the first point says so.
The founder is not named as such in the article; the facts box gives Qara Yusuf (independence 1410) and the earlier leaders Birdi Khwaja, Bayram Khwaja and Qara Mahammad.
The article says Qara Yusuf conquered Tabriz and executed 'Shaykh Uways Jalayir' in 1410; this is reproduced as written, though it is the same name as the sultan who defeated the tribe in 1366.
Qara Yusuf's death is given both as 1420 and December 1420; Jahan Shah's regnal dates as 1435–1467 (in the language section) and 1436–1467 (elsewhere): the profile uses 1436.
Left out for space: the etymological debate in detail, the Mamluk diplomatic letter of 1415 and most of the manuscript history.
